summary: Considers how X.500 relates to Internet and UK domains. It is an Experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes storing Internet domain information in an X.500 directory, where it can be searched and linked to organizational information. It describes an experimental way to connect the two naming systems, not a planned replacement for DNS.

subtitle: A proposal for representing domain records alongside organizational names in X.500.

tldr.problem: Domain names and organizational X.500 names describe different things, but users could benefit from finding related information together.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal stores domain components and DNS records in the X.500 directory tree, with attributes linking domain entries to organizational entries.
tldr.outcome: The memo proposes an experiment and explicitly says it is not intended to replace DNS operationally.

today: RFC 1279 is an Experimental memo proposing a directory experiment. It states that the approach was not intended as an operational replacement for DNS.

sections.title: Two Different Kinds of Names
sections.content:
DNS organizes domain names as a hierarchy and associates resource records with each name. X.500 provides a directory with structured names that can include country, organization, department, and person, plus a richer set of information.

The RFC treats organizational X.500 names as a layer above domain names, not as equivalent names. It proposes storing both structures in one directory information tree and connecting related entries with explicit attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS names locate domain information; X.500 names describe people and organizations. The proposal keeps these structures distinct but adds links between related entries.

sections.title: Representing Domains and Mailboxes
sections.content:
The RFC defines a DomainComponent attribute for each part of a domain name and object classes for domain entries and mailbox entries. The local part of a mailbox is represented as a final domain component, extending the same directory hierarchy.

A wildcard is represented by a domain component containing an asterisk. The RFC explains that a directory lookup may need to detect how many components match and then look up the wildcard form explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory stores each part of a domain name as its own component. It can also represent a mailbox as a domain-like entry, including a wildcard entry for matching names.

sections.title: DNS Records in the Directory
sections.content:
The proposal stores authoritative DNS records in a directory entry using one text attribute. The RFC chooses a text representation because it can be mapped to DNS and is straightforward for X.500 client software to handle.

It aims to preserve the DNS record information so data can move between the directory and DNS. It does not ask X.500 to reproduce DNS caching or time-to-live behavior, and it expects zone transfer or an equivalent process to maintain authoritative entries.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS records can be kept as text in directory entries, so a tool can transfer the information between X.500 and DNS. The directory does not take over DNS caching rules.

sections.title: Links, Uses, and Evaluation
sections.content:
Attributes connect a DNS-shaped entry to an organizational X.500 entry, and connect organizational entries back to domains. The RFC recommends keeping duplicate information to a minimum and using links when the same information already exists in the organizational tree.

The memo proposes pilot experiments to assess whether the approach is practical and useful. It says there was no current intention to provide an operational replacement for DNS, and it does not directly address security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Links let a user move between a domain entry and its related organization entry without copying all the information. The RFC asks for experiments and does not propose replacing DNS.
